Painted
pānt'ed
adj. and v. (coloured or adorned with pigment; in the prophets, the mark of the harlot and of vain self-adornment before judgment)
From Latin pingere, to paint. The Hebrew behind the prophetic uses is generally kachal (to paint the eyes with stibium) or sus/qara constructions rendered rentest thy face with painting.

Biblical Definition

The word arrives at a moment of doom. Jehu is at the gate, and “Jezebel heard of it; and she painted her face, and tired her head, and looked out at a window” (2 Kings 9:30). She is not preparing to escape but to meet her end in state, and within a few verses she is thrown from that window. Jeremiah turns the same picture into a national indictment: “Though thou clothest thyself with crimson, though thou deckest thee with ornaments of gold, though thou rentest thy face with painting, in vain shalt thou make thyself fair; thy lovers will despise thee, they will seek thy life” (Jeremiah 4:30). Ezekiel repeats it of Oholibah: “for whom thou didst wash thyself, paintedst thy eyes, and deckedst thyself with ornaments” (Ezekiel 23:40). In every case the painting is preparation for illicit alliance, and in every case it fails. There is also an ordinary use with no moral charge: the wicked king “cutteth him out windows; and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion” (Jeremiah 22:14) — where the sin named in the surrounding verses is building a house by unrighteousness and withholding a labourer's wages, not the colour of the walls.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines painting as the art of representing objects by colours, and to paint as to colour, and figuratively to adorn with specious but false appearances.

expand to see more

PAINT, v.t. To form a figure or likeness in colors; to lay colors on.

2. To represent in colors; as, to paint a face.

3. To color; to diversify with colors.

4. To lay on artificial color for ornament.

VERMILION, n. A beautiful red color, prepared from the sulphuret of mercury; used as a paint.

Key Scripture

2 Kings 9:30 — "And when Jehu was come to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it; and she painted her face, and tired her head, and looked out at a window."

Jeremiah 4:30 — "And when thou art spoiled, what wilt thou do? Though thou clothest thyself with crimson, though thou deckest thee with ornaments of gold, though thou rentest thy face with painting, in vain shalt thou make thyself fair; thy lovers will despise thee, they will seek thy life."

Ezekiel 23:40 — "And furthermore, that ye have sent for men to come from far, unto whom a messenger was sent; and, lo, they came: for whom thou didst wash thyself, paintedst thy eyes, and deckedst thyself with ornaments,"

Jeremiah 22:14 — "That saith, I will build me a wide house and large chambers, and cutteth him out windows; and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion."

Modern Corruption

The texts are made into a rule about cosmetics, when their subject is covenant unfaithfulness dressed up to meet its judgment.

expand to see more

Holiness movements of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries built a prohibition on these verses and made a painted face a test of fellowship. The passages will not carry it. Not one of them legislates about cosmetics; each describes a nation or a queen adorning herself for adulterous alliance at the moment judgment is arriving, and Jeremiah's point is explicitly the futility of the adornment — in vain shalt thou make thyself fair. To turn a prophetic indictment of covenant treachery into a dress code is to bind consciences where Scripture has not bound them, which the regulative principle forbids as strictly as it forbids inventing worship.

The real corruption these texts name is alive and has simply changed instruments. Jezebel painted her face to meet Jehu with her dignity intact; the modern equivalent is the curated presentation — the edited image, the managed reputation, the profile that shows a life no one is living. Jeremiah's verdict is the one that still applies: it is in vain, the lovers so courted will despise in the end, and the judgment arrives regardless of how the face is arranged. Scripture's alternative is not plainness as a rule but the hidden man of the heart, which is in the sight of God of great price.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kachal, to paint the eyes with stibium — 2 Kings 9:30, Ezekiel 23:40; pukh, the eye-paint itself; shashar, vermilion — Jeremiah 22:14.

expand to see more

Hebrew kachal — to paint the eyes; Ezekiel 23:40, and the practice behind 2 Kings 9:30.

Hebrew pukh — stibium, eye-paint; 2 Kings 9:30, Jeremiah 4:30, and the name of Job's daughter Keren-happuch, horn of eye-paint.

Hebrew shashar — vermilion; Jeremiah 22:14 and Ezekiel 23:14, a pigment for walls and images.

Jeremiah 4:30 supplies the verdict on the practice as the prophets use it: in vain shalt thou make thyself fair.

1 Peter 3:3-4 gives the New Testament counterpart — not the outward adorning, but the hidden man of the heart.

Usage

"“She painted her face, and tired her head, and looked out at a window” — and Jehu was already at the gate."

"“In vain shalt thou make thyself fair” — the prophetic verdict on the whole practice."

"The subject of these texts is treachery adorned, not cosmetics."
